summary:
Private, non-commercial sexual relations between consenting adults aged 16 and over have been lawful in Cuba since 1979, when the Social Defence Code that classified homosexual practices as a social threat was repealed. The offence of public display of homosexual condition was repealed in 1987, and the offence of bothering or soliciting with homosexual requests was narrowed in 1997 to cover sexual requests only. The Public Ostentation Law of 1938 was repealed in 1988, and police were instructed not to harass LGBT people.

Article 42 of the 2019 Constitution prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity and was the first Cuban constitutional text to name both grounds expressly. The definition of marriage as between a man and a woman in Article 36 was removed in the February 2019 referendum, with marriage redefined on the basis of free will and equality of rights.

The September 2022 Family Code referendum, the fourth national vote since 1959, produced legal recognition of marriage and unions between people of the same sex, adoption by same-sex couples, non-commercial surrogacy, legal gender change without surgery, shared parental rights and codified penalties for domestic violence.

The vote passed against organised religious opposition and a campaign by government opponents who voted No in order to deny the Díaz-Canel administration a victory amid the crackdown that followed the July 2021 protests, in which more than 1,400 people were arrested, and a period of record emigration. Opponents also argued that the child-welfare provisions could be turned against dissidents. The rights the Family Code recognises are contested rather than uniformly enforced.

Police enforcement has targeted gender presentation directly. In 2001 police ran a campaign against gay and trans people, preventing them from meeting in the street, imposing fines and closing meeting places. In 2004 police ran a campaign aimed at travestis, arresting those dressed in women's clothing; the crackdown in Havana that July involved detention, municipal warnings to stop dressing as women, sanctions against three people under the dangerousness law carrying up to four years' imprisonment, the closure of private clubs hosting their shows, a ban on gay parties, and refusal of entry to regular discos. Most of those affected were forced to wear men's clothing in public, and CENESEX advised against appearing in women's clothing until the crackdown passed.

Official institutions have campaigned for LGBT acceptance since the late 2000s. CENESEX runs a state-backed trans-rights programme that works with the police and the supreme court and carries out sexual-diversity education. Havana holds a pride march each May to mark the International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia and Transphobia, with attendance growing every year. Cuba voted to renew the mandate of the United Nations independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2016, 2019, 2022 and 2025.

State persecution of gay men dates to the UMAP forced-labour camps of 1965-68, where conscripts were sent to cut cane for around 60 hours a week in Camagüey, paid seven pesos a day, and subjected to electric-shock and injection experiments presented as cures. Official policy shifted during the mid-1970s, and in 2010 Fidel Castro publicly accepted blame for the persecution of gay Cubans in remarks carried by La Jornada.
tangentialFactors:
The legal framework is layered rather than consolidated. The labour-law amendment banning employment discrimination on sexual orientation was approved in December 2013, six years before the 2019 Constitution and nine years before the 2022 Family Code, so the three instruments sit at different stages of the same reform sequence.

Cuba has held only four national votes since 1959, the 2022 Family Code referendum among them, which places the equality settlement on a narrow base of direct popular endorsement rather than on routine legislative process.

Enforcement of the liberal framework has been episodic. The documented police campaigns against gender presentation date from 2001 and 2004; the 1988 repeal of the Public Ostentation Law and the order that police stop harassing LGBT people predate them; the Family Code followed in 2022. No source reviewed here records the current operational posture of the police toward gender-nonconforming people.
localsOnly:
Labor Code Law 116 bars discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity but does not list gender identity as a separate protected ground; its article 2(b) covers orientation and not identity. The amendment approved by lawmakers in December 2013 banned employment discrimination on sexual orientation after intense parliamentary debate. Mariela Castro of CENESEX proposed extending the ban to gender identity, disability and HIV status; the amendment that passed was the sexual-orientation ban, and the trans-specific extension was not the confirmed outcome. Claims that gender-identity discrimination is illegal in Cuba rest on Article 42 of the Constitution rather than on the Labor Code's enumerated grounds, so protection is uneven across instruments.

Transgender people have been permitted to serve openly in the Cuban Revolutionary Armed Forces since 1993, as have lesbian, gay and bisexual people. In 2012 Adela Hernández became the first known transgender person to hold public office in Cuba, elected as a delegate to the city council of Caibarien in Villa Clara province.

Trans healthcare is delivered through the public health system under Resolution 126 of 2008. CENESEX operates a state-backed programme that includes a trans-rights campaign and works with the police and the supreme court.

Citizens who leave to seek asylum abroad face prosecution on return. In January 2018 Victor Manuel Dueñas and Onasis Torres faced up to eight years in prison if they returned after filing asylum claims in the Netherlands, charged with treason against the homeland. A woman deported from the Netherlands was detained on 19 May 2018, and LGBTI activists, including Nelson Gandulla of the Cuban LGBTI Equality Foundation, remained under monitoring. Charges of this kind are brought against citizens who emigrate, not against visitors.
outOfScopeNotes:
No entry, visa, immigration-screening, airport-security or custody-search rule specific to trans travellers appears in the sources reviewed.

No record of police action against gender-nonconforming people after 2004 appears in the sources reviewed, and no account of current police practice on gender presentation is available.

No figure for trans-specific violence or homicide in Cuba appears in the sources reviewed, and no rate can be stated from them.

Whether the gender-identity, disability and HIV-status protections proposed in 2013 have since been enacted into the Labor Code is not established by these sources; the enumeration gap described above stands as the last confirmed position.

The administrative requirements, waiting periods and documentary conditions attached to legal gender change are referred to only as recognition without surgery; the procedure itself is not detailed.

No information on access by gender identity to bathrooms, changing facilities or other sex-segregated public facilities appears in the sources reviewed.
